Calendars === The way Rokuyō is presented and arranged in calendars reveals the following about the lunisolar calendar: * When one Rokuyō is omitted: ** The day following the omission is usually the first day (the new moon) of a normal (large) month, or it is the first day of an intercalary (small) month if the previous month was small. * When two Rokuyō are omitted: ** The day following the omission is the new moon of a normal month that was a small month. * When Rokuyō continue consecutively for 59 or 60 days: ** The preceding 30 days are from a normal (large) month, and the following 29 or 30 days are from an intercalary month. == Individual Rokuyō == Detailed explanations of each Rokuyō are as follows. The auspicious and inauspicious interpretations currently in use largely derive from the ''Ansei Miscellaneous Wankei Taisei'' (''{{ill|Kojirui-en|ja|古事類苑|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft}}''{{Cite web |title=National Diet Library Digital Collections |url=https://dl.ndl.go.jp/pid/1874246/1/67 |website=dl.ndl.go.jp |access-date=2024-03-31}}). === Senkachi === '''Senkachi''' (先勝 (せんしょう{{sfn|佐藤|1999|p=227}}, sen-kachi{{sfn|佐藤|1999|p=226}})) is considered a day on which it is advantageous to complete tasks early{{sfn|佐藤|1999|p=227}}. Its meaning is “he who acts first wins.” The morning is auspicious, while the afternoon is inauspicious{{sfn|佐藤|1999|p=227}}. It is deemed an auspicious day for handling urgent matters or legal proceedings{{sfn|佐藤|1999|p=227}}. In earlier times it was also written as “Sokki” or “Sokukichi.” === Tomobiki === {{redirect|Tomobiki|Previously, “Tomobiki exclusion” existed in the context of public sports betting (see {{ill|Tickets (Public Sports)|ja|公営競技|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft}}#History).}} '''Tomobiki''' (友引) is regarded as a day on which outcomes—whether favorable or unfavorable—remain undecided{{sfn|佐藤|1999|p=227}}; in some interpretations, the notion of “no win, no loss” or “drawing in friends” renders it auspicious. The term originates from the word “Ryūren” (立連), which originally meant “mutual drawing.” In the context of {{ill|Onmyōdō|ja|陰陽道|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft}}, it referred to days when conducting an activity in a certain direction might bring misfortune upon one’s friends, and this was later conflated with the concept of Tomobiki. The early morning and evening are considered auspicious, while midday is inauspicious{{sfn|佐藤|1999|p=227}}. There is a popular folk belief that funerals should be avoided on Tomobiki days{{sfn|佐藤|1999|p=227}}, as it is thought that holding a funeral on such a day will “draw one’s friends to the underworld” (i.e. lead to death). Consequently, funeral service providers and some crematoria may close on Tomobiki days. However, since Rokuyō is not inherently linked to Buddhism, some Buddhist sects (for example, Jōdo Shinshū) do perform funerals on Tomobiki days. Furthermore, some municipalities have abolished the practice of closing crematoria on Tomobiki days.{{Cite web2 |df=ja |title=Trial of Cremation on Tomobiki Day in Kawasaki City; Responding to an Era of Multiple Deaths |url=https://www.kanaloco.jp/news/government/entry-79466.html |website=神奈川新聞 |date=2016-08-03 |access-date=2024-03-11}}{{Cite web2 |df=ja |title=Deepening Cremation Wait Times in Winter; Chiba City Responds Even on Tomobiki Days |url=https://www3.nhk.or.jp/news/html/20231230/k10014303551000.html |website=NHK News |publisher=NHK |date=2023-12-30 |access-date=2024-03-11}} The superstition to avoid funerals on Tomobiki days is believed to have arisen from a confusion with “Tomobiki” (友曳), which originally referred to a custom of refraining from venturing in the direction indicated by the zodiac sign of that day. Because the sound is the same, the two became conflated. In contexts of celebration, the idea of “no win, no loss” is interpreted as signifying marital harmony; accordingly, some couples schedule their wedding receptions—or send out wedding favors as a “sharing of happiness”—on Tomobiki days. While the reading “Tomobiki” is now standard, its origin lies in the Chinese reading of “留引” as “yūin,” which was then adapted phonetically into Japanese as “Tomobiki,” and is unrelated to the literal meaning “to draw in friends.” The term “留引” originally indicated the persistence or stagnation of an event, suggesting that one should gauge the situation and act accordingly—continuing favorable circumstances or remedying unfavorable ones. === Senpu === {{nihongo|'''Senpu'''|せんぶ{{sfn|佐藤|1999|p=227}}, sen-make{{sfn|佐藤|1999|p=226}}}} is a day on which it is advisable to avoid urgent matters{{sfn|佐藤|1999|p=227}}. It is considered inauspicious for conflicts and official business, and is best suited for maintaining calm in all affairs{{sfn|佐藤|1999|p=227}}. Its meaning, “he who acts first loses,” serves as the counterpart to Senkachi{{sfn|佐藤|1999|p=227}}. The morning is regarded as inauspicious, while the afternoon is considered auspicious{{sfn|佐藤|1999|p=227}}. Originally, it was written as “Small fortune” or “Zhoukichi” and considered an auspicious day, but its present interpretation has prevailed. === Butsumetsu === '''Butsumetsu''' (仏滅) is deemed the most inauspicious day among the Rokuyō. Initially called “Kyobō” (虚亡)—meaning “void” or “no contest,” and also known as “Kūbō” (空亡)—this term later came to be interpreted as signifying the futility of all things, with the character for “Buddha” (仏) being applied to suggest that even the Buddha’s merits are absent{{sfn|佐藤|1999|p=227}}{{Cite Kotobank |word=Butsumetsu |encyclopedia=Heibonsha "Folk Dictionary" |accessdate=2024-03-11}}. However, historical records show that the term “Butsumetsu” first appears in the ''Banreki Ryōmenkan'' compiled in the fourth year of the Enkyō era (1747), while the term “Kyobō” first appears in the ''Ansei Miscellaneous Wankei Taisei'' (1854), prompting some criticism{{Sfn|小池|2021|pp=463-465}}. Butsumetsu is considered inauspicious for all matters{{sfn|佐藤|1999|p=227}}. It is the day on which celebratory events such as weddings are customarily avoided, and as a result some wedding venues offer discounts for ceremonies held on Butsumetsu. While other Rokuyō have multiple readings, Butsumetsu is read only as “butsumetsu.” Because its name includes the character for “Buddha,” it is often mistakenly assumed to represent the day on which the Buddha (Shakyamuni) attained nirvana (i.e. died). In a work from 1819 (''Bunsei Ni-U no Toshi, Nenchū Kiyōkun'uta Zen''), Butsumetsu is already explained as “the day of the Buddha’s death, and therefore unfavorable in every respect”{{sfn|小池|2021|pp=488-490}}. However, Rokuyō is not derived from Buddhism, and the fact that February 15 (lunar calendar)—traditionally regarded as the Buddha’s death anniversary—always falls on Butsumetsu in the lunisolar calendar is merely coincidental. It is also said that this is a day on which one should refrain from all activities, that illnesses tend to worsen, and that Buddhist rites should be avoided. An alternative interpretation under the name “Kyobō” holds that “when things perish and new ones begin, this day is more favorable for starting ventures than Taian.” === Taian === '''Taian''' (大安{{sfn|佐藤|1999|p=226}}) is considered an auspicious day for carrying out any undertaking{{sfn|佐藤|1999|p=227}}. Its name conveys the meaning “great peace and safety.” It is regarded as the most fortunate day among the Rokuyō, ensuring auspiciousness in every endeavor. Derived from the concept of “Tai'an,” many weddings and building ceremonies (such as the {{ill|Jōtōshiki|ja|上棟式|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft}}) are scheduled on Taian days. In addition, some people choose Taian for activities such as car registration, car delivery, construction work on building foundations, or house handovers. === Shakkō === '''Shakkō''' (赤口 (しゃっこう{{sfn|佐藤|1999|p=227}}, shakku{{sfn|佐藤|1999|p=226}})) is considered inauspicious for most of the day except around noon{{sfn|佐藤|1999|p=227}}. Only during the hour of {{ill|Go|ja|午|1=Horse (zodiac)|lt=Horse (午)|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft}} (roughly 11:00 AM to 1:00 PM) is it regarded as auspicious; at all other times, it is deemed inauspicious. It is believed that Shakkō emerged from a conflation of the {{ill|Akashaku-nichi|ja|赤舌日|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft}} of {{ill|Onmyōdō|ja|陰陽道|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft}} and a similar term (sometimes rendered as “Tai-akashaku”), wherein the deity presiding over the western gate of Jupiter (associated with Akashaku-nichi) and the deity presiding over the eastern gate (associated with Shakkō) were both considered inauspicious for legal disputes and contractual agreements{{sfn|佐藤|1999|p=227}}. Because the character for “red” is used in its name, this day is also thought to warn against dangers associated with fire and sharp objects – that is, anything that might symbolically evoke “death.” == Comparison Table of Lunisolar Calendar Dates and Rokuyō == {| class="wikitable" style="float:left;margin:0 1em 1em 0;text-align:right" ! colspan="6" style="background:#ccc" | {{ill|January (Lunisolar)|ja|1月 (旧暦)|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft}} |- ! revision.text:
{{Unreferenced|date=February 2021}} '''Rokuyō''' (六曜) is one of the {{ill|Calendar annotations|ja|暦注|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft}}. It comprises six types of day annotations: '''Senkachi''' (先勝 (せんしょう{{sfn|佐藤|1999|p=227}}, sen-kachi{{sfn|佐藤|1999|p=226}})) – '''Tomobiki''' (友引{{sfn|佐藤|1999|p=226}}) – '''Senpu''' (先負 (せんぷ, せんぶ{{sfn|佐藤|1999|p=227}}, sen-make{{sfn|佐藤|1999|p=226}})) – '''Butsumetsu''' (仏滅{{sfn|佐藤|1999|p=226}}) – '''Taian''' (大安{{sfn|佐藤|1999|p=226}}) – and '''Shakkō''' (赤口 (しゃっこう{{sfn|佐藤|1999|p=227}}, shakku{{sfn|佐藤|1999|p=226}})). == Overview == In {{ill|Japan|ja|日本|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft}}, Rokuyō is one of the most famous {{ill|Calendar|ja|暦|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft}} annotations and is often included in general {{ill|Calendar|ja|カレンダー|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft}} and planner ({{ill|Diary/Planner|ja|手帳|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft}}) publications. It continues to have influence in modern {{ill|Japan|ja|日本|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft}}, where it is linked with ceremonies such as weddings and funerals – for example, it is said that “weddings are best held on {{ill|Taian|ja|大安|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft}}” and “funerals should avoid {{ill|Tomobiki|ja|友引|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft}}.” In calendars based on the seven‐day week, the six annotations are usually printed in full (using two‐character kanji) rather than as abbreviations. However, some calendars highlight only Taian by printing its characters in red or by using a special symbol (such as a circle) to represent it, while omitting the other Rokuyō annotations. It is also known as '''Rokki''' (六輝) or '''Shukuyō''' (宿曜), though these names were coined after the {{ill|Meiji|ja|明治|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft}} era to avoid confusion with the seven‐day week system. Although terms such as Butsumetsu and Tomobiki appear to be associated with Buddhist rituals, they are not actually connected to Buddhism. Their seemingly Buddhist character is due to the use of ateji (phonetic substitutions). Since blind reliance on divination may cause one to neglect the essential aspects of a matter – often with adverse consequences – Buddhism rejects such practices. Moreover, in the {{ill|Japanese Buddhism|ja|日本仏教|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft}} of the Jōdo Shinshū sect, Shinran expounded in a {{ill|Wasan|ja|和讃|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft}} that “choosing days based on their auspiciousness or inauspiciousness is not advisable.” Thus, all superstitions and popular beliefs are repudiated, with the understanding that in Buddhism things are determined by causal relationships rather than by Rokuyō. == History == A popular legend claims that Rokuyō originated as the “Kōmei Rokki” conceived by {{ill|Zhuge Liang|ja|諸葛亮|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft}}, though it is doubtful that Rokuyō existed during the {{ill|Three Kingdoms period (China)|ja|三国時代 (中国)|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft}} ({{sfn|佐藤|1999|p=226}}). In general, Rokuyō is believed to have developed as a variation of the Chinese divination system known as {{ill|Liu Ren Divination|ja|六壬神課|lt=Liu Ren Divination|lt_ja=六壬|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft}}.{{Cite web |title=National Diet Library Digital Collections |url=https://dl.ndl.go.jp/pid/1246210/1/124 |website=dl.ndl.go.jp |access-date=2024-03-31}} The “Liu Ren Shikō” (六壬時課) was reportedly devised by {{ill|Li Chunfeng|ja|李淳風|lt=Li Chunfeng|lt_ja=李淳風|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft}} of the {{ill|Tang dynasty|ja|唐|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft}}, and was used to divine the auspiciousness of particular times (i.e. to determine the fortune of a given time period){{Sfn|小池|2021|p=446}}. In Li Chunfeng’s work, ''Rikujin Shōketsu'' (六壬承訣), the days designated include Taian, Ryūren, Sokki, Shakkō, Shōkichi, and Kūbō{{sfn|佐藤|1999|p=226}}. It is thought that Liu Ren Shikō was transmitted to Japan during the {{ill|Muromachi period|ja|室町時代|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft}}, though the details remain uncertain{{Sfn|小池|2021|p=446}}. In China, a day divination method derived from Liu Ren Shikō – known as “Small Liu Ren” (小六壬) – emerged, and was introduced in the {{ill|Qing dynasty|ja|清|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft}} through Chen Zhonghua’s ''Tōdoku Ruijōsho'' (通読類情書) (【1771】){{Sfn|小池|2021|p=457}}. {{ill|Tadao Iijima|ja|飯島忠夫|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft}} considered the Japanese Rokuyō to have evolved from Small Liu Ren. In the fifth year of the {{ill|Jōkyō era|ja|貞享|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft}} (1688), Koizumi Matsutaku (Koizumi Mitsuyasu)’s work 『[https://www.wul.waseda.ac.jp/kotenseki/html/bunko31/bunko31_e1341/index.html Atamae Chōreki]』 featured a diagram for determining auspicious days (“dai an soku kichi jitsu toru no koto”), which assigned Taian (auspicious), Ritsuren (inauspicious), Zokukichi (auspicious), Shakkō (inauspicious), Small fortune (auspicious), and Kyomō (inauspicious){{sfn|佐藤|1999|p=226}}. Although there is a difference between systems that designate auspiciousness for specific times and those that cover whole days, the sequence of annotations is identical to that found in Liu Ren Shikō{{Sfn|小池|2021|pp=447-449}}. The earliest recorded use of the term “Rokuyō” in Japan appears in the ninth year of the {{ill|Genroku period|ja|元禄|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft}} (1696) in a work known as ''Rokuyōshi'' (六曜私) attributed to {{ill|Myōhōin|ja|妙法院|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft}}{{Sfn|小池|2021|p=482}}. Although its relationship to the modern Rokuyō remains unclear, the text includes the terms “Senkachi”, “Tomobiki”, and “Senpu”, and is strongly colored by a syncretism of Shinto and Buddhism. According to research by {{ill|Shigenori Kanda|ja|神田茂|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft}}, the first appearance of the current form of Rokuyō appears to be in the compilation of ''Banreki Ryōmenkan'' (万暦両面鑑) in the fourth year of the {{ill|Enkyō era|ja|延享|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft}} (1747){{Sfn|小池|2021|p=453}}. Rokuyō |- ! 7th Century ! 1771 ! 1688 ! 1747 |- | January 1 / July 1 | Taian | Small fortune | Taian | Senkachi |- | February 1 / August 1 | Ryūren | Kūbō | Ritsuren | Tomobiki |- | March 1 / September 1 | Sokki | Taian | Zokukichi | Senpu |- | April 1 / October 1 | Shakkō | Ryūren | Shakkō | Butsumetsu |- | May 1 / November 1 | Shōkichi | Sokki | Small fortune | Taian |- | June 1 / December 1 | Kūbō | Shakkō | Kyomō | Shakkō |} == Distribution == Rokuyō follows a repeating cycle in the order “Senkachi → Tomobiki → Senpu → Butsumetsu → Taian → Shakkō.” However, in the lunisolar calendar the Rokuyō for the first day of each month is fixed as follows. In an intercalary month, the assignment remains the same as in the preceding month. {| class="wikitable" |- ! Lunisolar Month ! Rokuyō |- | {{ill|January (Lunisolar)|ja|1月 (旧暦)|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft}} / {{ill|July (Lunisolar)|ja|7月 (旧暦)|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft}} | Senkachi |- | {{ill|February (Lunisolar)|ja|2月 (旧暦)|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft}} / {{ill|August (Lunisolar)|ja|8月 (旧暦)|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft}} | Tomobiki |- | {{ill|March (Lunisolar)|ja|3月 (旧暦)|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft}} / {{ill|September (Lunisolar)|ja|9月 (旧暦)|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft}} | Senpu |- | {{ill|April (Lunisolar)|ja|4月 (旧暦)|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft}} / {{ill|Kannazuki|lt=October (Lunisolar)|ja|10月 (旧暦)|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft}} | Butsumetsu |- | {{ill|May (Lunisolar)|ja|5月 (旧暦)|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft}} / {{ill|November (Lunisolar)|ja|11月 (旧暦)|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft}} | Taian |- | {{ill|June (Lunisolar)|ja|6月 (旧暦)|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft}} / {{ill|December (Lunisolar)|ja|12月 (旧暦)|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft}} | Shakkō |} Thus, in the lunisolar calendar the Rokuyō is determined by the month and day. In essence, if the sum of the lunisolar month number and the day number is a multiple of 6, the day is Taian. However, in solar ({{ill|Solar calendar|ja|新暦|1=New Calendar (Japan)|lt=New Calendar|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft}}) calendars the once-regular cycle may suddenly break, and the Rokuyō for the same day can differ by year or month. This discrepancy between the lunisolar and solar calendars lends an air of mystery to Rokuyō, contributing to its continued use in ceremonial events such as weddings and funerals{{sfn|佐藤|1999|p=226}}. Calendars === The way Rokuyō is presented and arranged in calendars reveals the following about the lunisolar calendar: * When one Rokuyō is omitted: ** The day following the omission is usually the first day (the new moon) of a normal (large) month, or it is the first day of an intercalary (small) month if the previous month was small. * When two Rokuyō are omitted: ** The day following the omission is the new moon of a normal month that was a small month. * When Rokuyō continue consecutively for 59 or 60 days: ** The preceding 30 days are from a normal (large) month, and the following 29 or 30 days are from an intercalary month. == Individual Rokuyō == Detailed explanations of each Rokuyō are as follows. The auspicious and inauspicious interpretations currently in use largely derive from the ''Ansei Miscellaneous Wankei Taisei'' (''{{ill|Kojirui-en|ja|古事類苑|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft}}''{{Cite web |title=National Diet Library Digital Collections |url=https://dl.ndl.go.jp/pid/1874246/1/67 |website=dl.ndl.go.jp |access-date=2024-03-31}}). === Senkachi === '''Senkachi''' (先勝 (せんしょう{{sfn|佐藤|1999|p=227}}, sen-kachi{{sfn|佐藤|1999|p=226}})) is considered a day on which it is advantageous to complete tasks early{{sfn|佐藤|1999|p=227}}. Its meaning is “he who acts first wins.” The morning is auspicious, while the afternoon is inauspicious{{sfn|佐藤|1999|p=227}}. It is deemed an auspicious day for handling urgent matters or legal proceedings{{sfn|佐藤|1999|p=227}}. In earlier times it was also written as “Sokki” or “Sokukichi.” === Tomobiki === {{redirect|Tomobiki|Previously, “Tomobiki exclusion” existed in the context of public sports betting (see {{ill|Tickets (Public Sports)|ja|公営競技|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft}}#History).}} '''Tomobiki''' (友引) is regarded as a day on which outcomes—whether favorable or unfavorable—remain undecided{{sfn|佐藤|1999|p=227}}; in some interpretations, the notion of “no win, no loss” or “drawing in friends” renders it auspicious. The term originates from the word “Ryūren” (立連), which originally meant “mutual drawing.” In the context of {{ill|Onmyōdō|ja|陰陽道|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft}}, it referred to days when conducting an activity in a certain direction might bring misfortune upon one’s friends, and this was later conflated with the concept of Tomobiki. The early morning and evening are considered auspicious, while midday is inauspicious{{sfn|佐藤|1999|p=227}}. There is a popular folk belief that funerals should be avoided on Tomobiki days{{sfn|佐藤|1999|p=227}}, as it is thought that holding a funeral on such a day will “draw one’s friends to the underworld” (i.e. lead to death). Consequently, funeral service providers and some crematoria may close on Tomobiki days. However, since Rokuyō is not inherently linked to Buddhism, some Buddhist sects (for example, Jōdo Shinshū) do perform funerals on Tomobiki days. Furthermore, some municipalities have abolished the practice of closing crematoria on Tomobiki days.{{Cite web2 |df=ja |title=Trial of Cremation on Tomobiki Day in Kawasaki City; Responding to an Era of Multiple Deaths |url=https://www.kanaloco.jp/news/government/entry-79466.html |website=神奈川新聞 |date=2016-08-03 |access-date=2024-03-11}}{{Cite web2 |df=ja |title=Deepening Cremation Wait Times in Winter; Chiba City Responds Even on Tomobiki Days |url=https://www3.nhk.or.jp/news/html/20231230/k10014303551000.html |website=NHK News |publisher=NHK |date=2023-12-30 |access-date=2024-03-11}} The superstition to avoid funerals on Tomobiki days is believed to have arisen from a confusion with “Tomobiki” (友曳), which originally referred to a custom of refraining from venturing in the direction indicated by the zodiac sign of that day. Because the sound is the same, the two became conflated. In contexts of celebration, the idea of “no win, no loss” is interpreted as signifying marital harmony; accordingly, some couples schedule their wedding receptions—or send out wedding favors as a “sharing of happiness”—on Tomobiki days. While the reading “Tomobiki” is now standard, its origin lies in the Chinese reading of “留引” as “yūin,” which was then adapted phonetically into Japanese as “Tomobiki,” and is unrelated to the literal meaning “to draw in friends.” The term “留引” originally indicated the persistence or stagnation of an event, suggesting that one should gauge the situation and act accordingly—continuing favorable circumstances or remedying unfavorable ones. === Senpu === {{nihongo|'''Senpu'''|せんぶ{{sfn|佐藤|1999|p=227}}, sen-make{{sfn|佐藤|1999|p=226}}}} is a day on which it is advisable to avoid urgent matters{{sfn|佐藤|1999|p=227}}. It is considered inauspicious for conflicts and official business, and is best suited for maintaining calm in all affairs{{sfn|佐藤|1999|p=227}}. Its meaning, “he who acts first loses,” serves as the counterpart to Senkachi{{sfn|佐藤|1999|p=227}}. The morning is regarded as inauspicious, while the afternoon is considered auspicious{{sfn|佐藤|1999|p=227}}. Originally, it was written as “Small fortune” or “Zhoukichi” and considered an auspicious day, but its present interpretation has prevailed. === Butsumetsu === '''Butsumetsu''' (仏滅) is deemed the most inauspicious day among the Rokuyō. Initially called “Kyobō” (虚亡)—meaning “void” or “no contest,” and also known as “Kūbō” (空亡)—this term later came to be interpreted as signifying the futility of all things, with the character for “Buddha” (仏) being applied to suggest that even the Buddha’s merits are absent{{sfn|佐藤|1999|p=227}}{{Cite Kotobank |word=Butsumetsu |encyclopedia=Heibonsha "Folk Dictionary" |accessdate=2024-03-11}}. However, historical records show that the term “Butsumetsu” first appears in the ''Banreki Ryōmenkan'' compiled in the fourth year of the Enkyō era (1747), while the term “Kyobō” first appears in the ''Ansei Miscellaneous Wankei Taisei'' (1854), prompting some criticism{{Sfn|小池|2021|pp=463-465}}. Butsumetsu is considered inauspicious for all matters{{sfn|佐藤|1999|p=227}}. It is the day on which celebratory events such as weddings are customarily avoided, and as a result some wedding venues offer discounts for ceremonies held on Butsumetsu. While other Rokuyō have multiple readings, Butsumetsu is read only as “butsumetsu.” Because its name includes the character for “Buddha,” it is often mistakenly assumed to represent the day on which the Buddha (Shakyamuni) attained nirvana (i.e. died). In a work from 1819 (''Bunsei Ni-U no Toshi, Nenchū Kiyōkun'uta Zen''), Butsumetsu is already explained as “the day of the Buddha’s death, and therefore unfavorable in every respect”{{sfn|小池|2021|pp=488-490}}. However, Rokuyō is not derived from Buddhism, and the fact that February 15 (lunar calendar)—traditionally regarded as the Buddha’s death anniversary—always falls on Butsumetsu in the lunisolar calendar is merely coincidental. It is also said that this is a day on which one should refrain from all activities, that illnesses tend to worsen, and that Buddhist rites should be avoided. An alternative interpretation under the name “Kyobō” holds that “when things perish and new ones begin, this day is more favorable for starting ventures than Taian.” === Taian === '''Taian''' (大安{{sfn|佐藤|1999|p=226}}) is considered an auspicious day for carrying out any undertaking{{sfn|佐藤|1999|p=227}}. Its name conveys the meaning “great peace and safety.” It is regarded as the most fortunate day among the Rokuyō, ensuring auspiciousness in every endeavor. Derived from the concept of “Tai'an,” many weddings and building ceremonies (such as the {{ill|Jōtōshiki|ja|上棟式|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft}}) are scheduled on Taian days. In addition, some people choose Taian for activities such as car registration, car delivery, construction work on building foundations, or house handovers. === Shakkō === '''Shakkō''' (赤口 (しゃっこう{{sfn|佐藤|1999|p=227}}, shakku{{sfn|佐藤|1999|p=226}})) is considered inauspicious for most of the day except around noon{{sfn|佐藤|1999|p=227}}. Only during the hour of {{ill|Go|ja|午|1=Horse (zodiac)|lt=Horse (午)|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft}} (roughly 11:00 AM to 1:00 PM) is it regarded as auspicious; at all other times, it is deemed inauspicious. It is believed that Shakkō emerged from a conflation of the {{ill|Akashaku-nichi|ja|赤舌日|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft}} of {{ill|Onmyōdō|ja|陰陽道|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft}} and a similar term (sometimes rendered as “Tai-akashaku”), wherein the deity presiding over the western gate of Jupiter (associated with Akashaku-nichi) and the deity presiding over the eastern gate (associated with Shakkō) were both considered inauspicious for legal disputes and contractual agreements{{sfn|佐藤|1999|p=227}}. Because the character for “red” is used in its name, this day is also thought to warn against dangers associated with fire and sharp objects – that is, anything that might symbolically evoke “death.” == Comparison Table of Lunisolar Calendar Dates and Rokuyō == {| class="wikitable" style="float:left;margin:0 1em 1em 0;text-align:right" ! colspan="6" style="background:#ccc" | {{ill|January (Lunisolar)|ja|1月 (旧暦)|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft}} |- ! revision.text:
{{Unreferenced|date=February 2021}} '''Rokuyō''' (六曜) is one of the {{ill|Calendar annotations|ja|暦注|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft}}. It comprises six types of day annotations: '''Senkachi''' (先勝 (せんしょう{{sfn|佐藤|1999|p=227}}, sen-kachi{{sfn|佐藤|1999|p=226}})) – '''Tomobiki''' (友引{{sfn|佐藤|1999|p=226}}) – '''Senpu''' (先負 (せんぷ, せんぶ{{sfn|佐藤|1999|p=227}}, sen-make{{sfn|佐藤|1999|p=226}})) – '''Butsumetsu''' (仏滅{{sfn|佐藤|1999|p=226}}) – '''Taian''' (大安{{sfn|佐藤|1999|p=226}}) – and '''Shakkō''' (赤口 (しゃっこう{{sfn|佐藤|1999|p=227}}, shakku{{sfn|佐藤|1999|p=226}})). == Overview == In {{ill|Japan|ja|日本|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft}}, Rokuyō is one of the most famous {{ill|Calendar|ja|暦|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft}} annotations and is often included in general {{ill|Calendar|ja|カレンダー|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft}} and planner ({{ill|Diary/Planner|ja|手帳|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft}}) publications. It continues to have influence in modern {{ill|Japan|ja|日本|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft}}, where it is linked with ceremonies such as weddings and funerals – for example, it is said that “weddings are best held on {{ill|Taian|ja|大安|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft}}” and “funerals should avoid {{ill|Tomobiki|ja|友引|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft}}.” In calendars based on the seven‐day week, the six annotations are usually printed in full (using two‐character kanji) rather than as abbreviations. However, some calendars highlight only Taian by printing its characters in red or by using a special symbol (such as a circle) to represent it, while omitting the other Rokuyō annotations. It is also known as '''Rokki''' (六輝) or '''Shukuyō''' (宿曜), though these names were coined after the {{ill|Meiji|ja|明治|1=Meiji era|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft}} era to avoid confusion with the seven‐day week system. Although terms such as Butsumetsu and Tomobiki appear to be associated with Buddhist rituals, they are not actually connected to Buddhism. Their seemingly Buddhist character is due to the use of ateji (phonetic substitutions). Since blind reliance on divination may cause one to neglect the essential aspects of a matter – often with adverse consequences – Buddhism rejects such practices. Moreover, in the {{ill|Japanese Buddhism|ja|日本仏教|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft}} of the Jōdo Shinshū sect, Shinran expounded in a {{ill|Wasan|ja|和讃|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft}} that “choosing days based on their auspiciousness or inauspiciousness is not advisable.” Thus, all superstitions and popular beliefs are repudiated, with the understanding that in Buddhism things are determined by causal relationships rather than by Rokuyō. == History == A popular legend claims that Rokuyō originated as the “Kōmei Rokki” conceived by {{ill|Zhuge Liang|ja|諸葛亮|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft}}, though it is doubtful that Rokuyō existed during the {{ill|Three Kingdoms period (China)|ja|三国時代 (中国)|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft}} ({{sfn|佐藤|1999|p=226}}). In general, Rokuyō is believed to have developed as a variation of the Chinese divination system known as {{ill|Liu Ren Divination|ja|六壬神課|lt=Liu Ren Divination|lt_ja=六壬|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft}}.{{Cite web |title=National Diet Library Digital Collections |url=https://dl.ndl.go.jp/pid/1246210/1/124 |website=dl.ndl.go.jp |access-date=2024-03-31}} The “Liu Ren Shikō” (六壬時課) was reportedly devised by {{ill|Li Chunfeng|ja|李淳風|lt=Li Chunfeng|lt_ja=李淳風|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft}} of the {{ill|Tang dynasty|ja|唐|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft}}, and was used to divine the auspiciousness of particular times (i.e. to determine the fortune of a given time period){{Sfn|小池|2021|p=446}}. In Li Chunfeng’s work, ''Rikujin Shōketsu'' (六壬承訣), the days designated include Taian, Ryūren, Sokki, Shakkō, Shōkichi, and Kūbō{{sfn|佐藤|1999|p=226}}. It is thought that Liu Ren Shikō was transmitted to Japan during the {{ill|Muromachi period|ja|室町時代|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft}}, though the details remain uncertain{{Sfn|小池|2021|p=446}}. In China, a day divination method derived from Liu Ren Shikō – known as “Small Liu Ren” (小六壬) – emerged, and was introduced in the {{ill|Qing dynasty|ja|清|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft}} through Chen Zhonghua’s ''Tōdoku Ruijōsho'' (通読類情書) (【1771】){{Sfn|小池|2021|p=457}}. {{ill|Tadao Iijima|ja|飯島忠夫|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft}} considered the Japanese Rokuyō to have evolved from Small Liu Ren. In the fifth year of the {{ill|Jōkyō era|ja|貞享|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft}} (1688), Koizumi Matsutaku (Koizumi Mitsuyasu)’s work 『[https://www.wul.waseda.ac.jp/kotenseki/html/bunko31/bunko31_e1341/index.html Atamae Chōreki]』 featured a diagram for determining auspicious days (“dai an soku kichi jitsu toru no koto”), which assigned Taian (auspicious), Ritsuren (inauspicious), Zokukichi (auspicious), Shakkō (inauspicious), Small fortune (auspicious), and Kyomō (inauspicious){{sfn|佐藤|1999|p=226}}. Although there is a difference between systems that designate auspiciousness for specific times and those that cover whole days, the sequence of annotations is identical to that found in Liu Ren Shikō{{Sfn|小池|2021|pp=447-449}}. The earliest recorded use of the term “Rokuyō” in Japan appears in the ninth year of the {{ill|Genroku period|ja|元禄|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft}} (1696) in a work known as ''Rokuyōshi'' (六曜私) attributed to {{ill|Myōhōin|ja|妙法院|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft}}{{Sfn|小池|2021|p=482}}. Although its relationship to the modern Rokuyō remains unclear, the text includes the terms “Senkachi”, “Tomobiki”, and “Senpu”, and is strongly colored by a syncretism of Shinto and Buddhism. According to research by {{ill|Shigenori Kanda|ja|神田茂|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft}}, the first appearance of the current form of Rokuyō appears to be in the compilation of ''Banreki Ryōmenkan'' (万暦両面鑑) in the fourth year of the {{ill|Enkyō era|ja|延享|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft}} (1747){{Sfn|小池|2021|p=453}}. The assignments for dates in these examples are summarized in the following table: {| class="wikitable" |+ ! rowspan="2" | Lunisolar Calendar Date ! Liu Ren Shikō (time segments) ! Small Liu Ren ! Taian-based Auspicious Day Selection ! Rokuyō |- ! 7th Century ! 1771 ! 1688 ! 1747 |- | January 1 / July 1 | Taian | Small fortune | Taian | Senkachi |- | February 1 / August 1 | Ryūren | Kūbō | Ritsuren | Tomobiki |- | March 1 / September 1 | Sokki | Taian | Zokukichi | Senpu |- | April 1 / October 1 | Shakkō | Ryūren | Shakkō | Butsumetsu |- | May 1 / November 1 | Shōkichi | Sokki | Small fortune | Taian |- | June 1 / December 1 | Kūbō | Shakkō | Kyomō | Shakkō |} == Distribution == Rokuyō follows a repeating cycle in the order “Senkachi → Tomobiki → Senpu → Butsumetsu → Taian → Shakkō.” However, in the lunisolar calendar the Rokuyō for the first day of each month is fixed as follows. In an intercalary month, the assignment remains the same as in the preceding month. {| class="wikitable" |- ! Lunisolar Month ! Rokuyō |- | {{ill|January (Lunisolar)|ja|1月 (旧暦)|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft}} / {{ill|July (Lunisolar)|ja|7月 (旧暦)|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft}} | Senkachi |- | {{ill|February (Lunisolar)|ja|2月 (旧暦)|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft}} / {{ill|August (Lunisolar)|ja|8月 (旧暦)|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft}} | Tomobiki |- | {{ill|March (Lunisolar)|ja|3月 (旧暦)|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft}} / {{ill|September (Lunisolar)|ja|9月 (旧暦)|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft}} | Senpu |- | {{ill|April (Lunisolar)|ja|4月 (旧暦)|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft}} / {{ill|Kannazuki|lt=October (Lunisolar)|ja|10月 (旧暦)|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft}} | Butsumetsu |- | {{ill|May (Lunisolar)|ja|5月 (旧暦)|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft}} / {{ill|November (Lunisolar)|ja|11月 (旧暦)|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft}} | Taian |- | {{ill|June (Lunisolar)|ja|6月 (旧暦)|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft}} / {{ill|December (Lunisolar)|ja|12月 (旧暦)|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft}} | Shakkō |} Thus, in the lunisolar calendar the Rokuyō is determined by the month and day. In essence, if the sum of the lunisolar month number and the day number is a multiple of 6, the day is Taian. However, in solar ({{ill|Solar calendar|ja|新暦|1=New Calendar (Japan)|lt=New Calendar|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft}}) calendars the once-regular cycle may suddenly break, and the Rokuyō for the same day can differ by year or month. This discrepancy between the lunisolar and solar calendars lends an air of mystery to Rokuyō, contributing to its continued use in ceremonial events such as weddings and funerals{{sfn|佐藤|1999|p=226}}. Calendars === The way Rokuyō is presented and arranged in calendars reveals the following about the lunisolar calendar: * When one Rokuyō is omitted: ** The day following the omission is usually the first day (the new moon) of a normal (large) month, or it is the first day of an intercalary (small) month if the previous month was small. * When two Rokuyō are omitted: ** The day following the omission is the new moon of a normal month that was a small month. * When Rokuyō continue consecutively for 59 or 60 days: ** The preceding 30 days are from a normal (large) month, and the following 29 or 30 days are from an intercalary month. == Individual Rokuyō == Detailed explanations of each Rokuyō are as follows. The auspicious and inauspicious interpretations currently in use largely derive from the ''Ansei Miscellaneous Wankei Taisei'' (''{{ill|Kojirui-en|ja|古事類苑|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft}}''{{Cite web |title=National Diet Library Digital Collections |url=https://dl.ndl.go.jp/pid/1874246/1/67 |website=dl.ndl.go.jp |access-date=2024-03-31}}). === Senkachi === '''Senkachi''' (先勝 (せんしょう{{sfn|佐藤|1999|p=227}}, sen-kachi{{sfn|佐藤|1999|p=226}})) is considered a day on which it is advantageous to complete tasks early{{sfn|佐藤|1999|p=227}}. Its meaning is “he who acts first wins.” The morning is auspicious, while the afternoon is inauspicious{{sfn|佐藤|1999|p=227}}. It is deemed an auspicious day for handling urgent matters or legal proceedings{{sfn|佐藤|1999|p=227}}. In earlier times it was also written as “Sokki” or “Sokukichi.” === Tomobiki === {{redirect|Tomobiki|Previously, “Tomobiki exclusion” existed in the context of public sports betting (see {{ill|Tickets (Public Sports)|ja|公営競技|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft}}#History).}} '''Tomobiki''' (友引) is regarded as a day on which outcomes—whether favorable or unfavorable—remain undecided{{sfn|佐藤|1999|p=227}}; in some interpretations, the notion of “no win, no loss” or “drawing in friends” renders it auspicious. The term originates from the word “Ryūren” (立連), which originally meant “mutual drawing.” In the context of {{ill|Onmyōdō|ja|陰陽道|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft}}, it referred to days when conducting an activity in a certain direction might bring misfortune upon one’s friends, and this was later conflated with the concept of Tomobiki. The early morning and evening are considered auspicious, while midday is inauspicious{{sfn|佐藤|1999|p=227}}. There is a popular folk belief that funerals should be avoided on Tomobiki days{{sfn|佐藤|1999|p=227}}, as it is thought that holding a funeral on such a day will “draw one’s friends to the underworld” (i.e. lead to death). Consequently, funeral service providers and some crematoria may close on Tomobiki days. However, since Rokuyō is not inherently linked to Buddhism, some Buddhist sects (for example, Jōdo Shinshū) do perform funerals on Tomobiki days. Furthermore, some municipalities have abolished the practice of closing crematoria on Tomobiki days.{{Cite web2 |df=ja |title=Trial of Cremation on Tomobiki Day in Kawasaki City; Responding to an Era of Multiple Deaths |url=https://www.kanaloco.jp/news/government/entry-79466.html |website=神奈川新聞 |date=2016-08-03 |access-date=2024-03-11}}{{Cite web2 |df=ja |title=Deepening Cremation Wait Times in Winter; Chiba City Responds Even on Tomobiki Days |url=https://www3.nhk.or.jp/news/html/20231230/k10014303551000.html |website=NHK News |publisher=NHK |date=2023-12-30 |access-date=2024-03-11}} The superstition to avoid funerals on Tomobiki days is believed to have arisen from a confusion with “Tomobiki” (友曳), which originally referred to a custom of refraining from venturing in the direction indicated by the zodiac sign of that day. Because the sound is the same, the two became conflated. In contexts of celebration, the idea of “no win, no loss” is interpreted as signifying marital harmony; accordingly, some couples schedule their wedding receptions—or send out wedding favors as a “sharing of happiness”—on Tomobiki days. While the reading “Tomobiki” is now standard, its origin lies in the Chinese reading of “留引” as “yūin,” which was then adapted phonetically into Japanese as “Tomobiki,” and is unrelated to the literal meaning “to draw in friends.” The term “留引” originally indicated the persistence or stagnation of an event, suggesting that one should gauge the situation and act accordingly—continuing favorable circumstances or remedying unfavorable ones. === Senpu === {{nihongo|'''Senpu'''|せんぶ{{sfn|佐藤|1999|p=227}}, sen-make{{sfn|佐藤|1999|p=226}}}} is a day on which it is advisable to avoid urgent matters{{sfn|佐藤|1999|p=227}}. It is considered inauspicious for conflicts and official business, and is best suited for maintaining calm in all affairs{{sfn|佐藤|1999|p=227}}. Its meaning, “he who acts first loses,” serves as the counterpart to Senkachi{{sfn|佐藤|1999|p=227}}. The morning is regarded as inauspicious, while the afternoon is considered auspicious{{sfn|佐藤|1999|p=227}}. Originally, it was written as “Small fortune” or “Zhoukichi” and considered an auspicious day, but its present interpretation has prevailed. === Butsumetsu === '''Butsumetsu''' (仏滅) is deemed the most inauspicious day among the Rokuyō. Initially called “Kyobō” (虚亡)—meaning “void” or “no contest,” and also known as “Kūbō” (空亡)—this term later came to be interpreted as signifying the futility of all things, with the character for “Buddha” (仏) being applied to suggest that even the Buddha’s merits are absent{{sfn|佐藤|1999|p=227}}{{Cite Kotobank |word=Butsumetsu |encyclopedia=Heibonsha "Folk Dictionary" |accessdate=2024-03-11}}. However, historical records show that the term “Butsumetsu” first appears in the ''Banreki Ryōmenkan'' compiled in the fourth year of the Enkyō era (1747), while the term “Kyobō” first appears in the ''Ansei Miscellaneous Wankei Taisei'' (1854), prompting some criticism{{Sfn|小池|2021|pp=463-465}}. Butsumetsu is considered inauspicious for all matters{{sfn|佐藤|1999|p=227}}. It is the day on which celebratory events such as weddings are customarily avoided, and as a result some wedding venues offer discounts for ceremonies held on Butsumetsu. While other Rokuyō have multiple readings, Butsumetsu is read only as “butsumetsu.” Because its name includes the character for “Buddha,” it is often mistakenly assumed to represent the day on which the Buddha (Shakyamuni) attained nirvana (i.e. died). In a work from 1819 (''Bunsei Ni-U no Toshi, Nenchū Kiyōkun'uta Zen''), Butsumetsu is already explained as “the day of the Buddha’s death, and therefore unfavorable in every respect”{{sfn|小池|2021|pp=488-490}}. However, Rokuyō is not derived from Buddhism, and the fact that February 15 (lunar calendar)—traditionally regarded as the Buddha’s death anniversary—always falls on Butsumetsu in the lunisolar calendar is merely coincidental. It is also said that this is a day on which one should refrain from all activities, that illnesses tend to worsen, and that Buddhist rites should be avoided. An alternative interpretation under the name “Kyobō” holds that “when things perish and new ones begin, this day is more favorable for starting ventures than Taian.” === Taian === '''Taian''' (大安{{sfn|佐藤|1999|p=226}}) is considered an auspicious day for carrying out any undertaking{{sfn|佐藤|1999|p=227}}. Its name conveys the meaning “great peace and safety.” It is regarded as the most fortunate day among the Rokuyō, ensuring auspiciousness in every endeavor. Derived from the concept of “Tai'an,” many weddings and building ceremonies (such as the {{ill|Jōtōshiki|ja|上棟式|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft}}) are scheduled on Taian days. In addition, some people choose Taian for activities such as car registration, car delivery, construction work on building foundations, or house handovers. === Shakkō === '''Shakkō''' (赤口 (しゃっこう{{sfn|佐藤|1999|p=227}}, shakku{{sfn|佐藤|1999|p=226}})) is considered inauspicious for most of the day except around noon{{sfn|佐藤|1999|p=227}}. Only during the hour of {{ill|Go|ja|午|1=Horse (zodiac)|lt=Horse (午)|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft}} (roughly 11:00 AM to 1:00 PM) is it regarded as auspicious; at all other times, it is deemed inauspicious. It is believed that Shakkō emerged from a conflation of the {{ill|Akashaku-nichi|ja|赤舌日|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft}} of {{ill|Onmyōdō|ja|陰陽道|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft}} and a similar term (sometimes rendered as “Tai-akashaku”), wherein the deity presiding over the western gate of Jupiter (associated with Akashaku-nichi) and the deity presiding over the eastern gate (associated with Shakkō) were both considered inauspicious for legal disputes and contractual agreements{{sfn|佐藤|1999|p=227}}. Because the character for “red” is used in its name, this day is also thought to warn against dangers associated with fire and sharp objects – that is, anything that might symbolically evoke “death.” == Comparison Table of Lunisolar Calendar Dates and Rokuyō == {| class="wikitable" style="float:left;margin:0 1em 1em 0;text-align:right" ! colspan="6" style="background:#ccc" | {{ill|January (Lunisolar)|ja|1月 (旧暦)|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft}} |- ! {{Unreferenced|date=February 2021}} '''Rokuyō''' (六曜) is one of the {{ill|Calendar annotations|ja|暦注|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft}}. It comprises six types of day annotations: '''Senkachi''' (先勝 (せんしょう{{sfn|佐藤|1999|p=227}}, sen-kachi{{sfn|佐藤|1999|p=226}})) – '''Tomobiki''' (友引{{sfn|佐藤|1999|p=226}}) – '''Senpu''' (先負 (せんぷ, せんぶ{{sfn|佐藤|1999|p=227}}, sen-make{{sfn|佐藤|1999|p=226}})) – '''Butsumetsu''' (仏滅{{sfn|佐藤|1999|p=226}}) – '''Taian''' (大安{{sfn|佐藤|1999|p=226}}) – and '''Shakkō''' (赤口 (しゃっこう{{sfn|佐藤|1999|p=227}}, shakku{{sfn|佐藤|1999|p=226}})). == Overview == In {{ill|Japan|ja|日本|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft}}, Rokuyō is one of the most famous {{ill|Calendar|ja|暦|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft}} annotations and is often included in general {{ill|Calendar|ja|カレンダー|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft}} and planner ({{ill|Diary/Planner|ja|手帳|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft}}) publications. It continues to have influence in modern {{ill|Japan|ja|日本|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft}}, where it is linked with ceremonies such as weddings and funerals – for example, it is said that “weddings are best held on {{ill|Taian|ja|大安|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft}}” and “funerals should avoid {{ill|Tomobiki|ja|友引|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft}}.” In calendars based on the seven‐day week, the six annotations are usually printed in full (using two‐character kanji) rather than as abbreviations. However, some calendars highlight only Taian by printing its characters in red or by using a special symbol (such as a circle) to represent it, while omitting the other Rokuyō annotations. It is also known as '''Rokki''' (六輝) or '''Shukuyō''' (宿曜), though these names were coined after the {{ill|Meiji|ja|明治|1=Meiji era|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft}} era to avoid confusion with the seven‐day week system. Although terms such as Butsumetsu and Tomobiki appear to be associated with Buddhist rituals, they are not actually connected to Buddhism. Their seemingly Buddhist character is due to the use of ateji (phonetic substitutions). Since blind reliance on divination may cause one to neglect the essential aspects of a matter – often with adverse consequences – Buddhism rejects such practices. Moreover, in the {{ill|Japanese Buddhism|ja|日本仏教|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft}} of the Jōdo Shinshū sect, Shinran expounded in a {{ill|Wasan|ja|和讃|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft}} that “choosing days based on their auspiciousness or inauspiciousness is not advisable.” Thus, all superstitions and popular beliefs are repudiated, with the understanding that in Buddhism things are determined by causal relationships rather than by Rokuyō. == History == A popular legend claims that Rokuyō originated as the “Kōmei Rokki” conceived by {{ill|Zhuge Liang|ja|諸葛亮|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft}}, though it is doubtful that Rokuyō existed during the {{ill|Three Kingdoms period (China)|ja|三国時代 (中国)|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft}} ({{sfn|佐藤|1999|p=226}}). In general, Rokuyō is believed to have developed as a variation of the Chinese divination system known as {{ill|Liu Ren Divination|ja|六壬神課|lt=Liu Ren Divination|lt_ja=六壬|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft}}.{{Cite web |title=National Diet Library Digital Collections |url=https://dl.ndl.go.jp/pid/1246210/1/124 |website=dl.ndl.go.jp |access-date=2024-03-31}} The “Liu Ren Shikō” (六壬時課) was reportedly devised by {{ill|Li Chunfeng|ja|李淳風|lt=Li Chunfeng|lt_ja=李淳風|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft}} of the {{ill|Tang dynasty|ja|唐|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft}}, and was used to divine the auspiciousness of particular times (i.e. to determine the fortune of a given time period){{Sfn|小池|2021|p=446}}. In Li Chunfeng’s work, ''Rikujin Shōketsu'' (六壬承訣), the days designated include Taian, Ryūren, Sokki, Shakkō, Shōkichi, and Kūbō{{sfn|佐藤|1999|p=226}}. It is thought that Liu Ren Shikō was transmitted to Japan during the {{ill|Muromachi period|ja|室町時代|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft}}, though the details remain uncertain{{Sfn|小池|2021|p=446}}. In China, a day divination method derived from Liu Ren Shikō – known as “Small Liu Ren” (小六壬) – emerged, and was introduced in the {{ill|Qing dynasty|ja|清|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft}} through Chen Zhonghua’s ''Tōdoku Ruijōsho'' (通読類情書) (【1771】){{Sfn|小池|2021|p=457}}. {{ill|Tadao Iijima|ja|飯島忠夫|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft}} considered the Japanese Rokuyō to have evolved from Small Liu Ren. In the fifth year of the {{ill|Jōkyō era|ja|貞享|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft}} (1688), Koizumi Matsutaku (Koizumi Mitsuyasu)’s work 『[https://www.wul.waseda.ac.jp/kotenseki/html/bunko31/bunko31_e1341/index.html Atamae Chōreki]』 featured a diagram for determining auspicious days (“dai an soku kichi jitsu toru no koto”), which assigned Taian (auspicious), Ritsuren (inauspicious), Zokukichi (auspicious), Shakkō (inauspicious), Small fortune (auspicious), and Kyomō (inauspicious){{sfn|佐藤|1999|p=226}}. Although there is a difference between systems that designate auspiciousness for specific times and those that cover whole days, the sequence of annotations is identical to that found in Liu Ren Shikō{{Sfn|小池|2021|pp=447-449}}. The earliest recorded use of the term “Rokuyō” in Japan appears in the ninth year of the {{ill|Genroku period|ja|元禄|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft}} (1696) in a work known as ''Rokuyōshi'' (六曜私) attributed to {{ill|Myōhōin|ja|妙法院|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft}}{{Sfn|小池|2021|p=482}}. Although its relationship to the modern Rokuyō remains unclear, the text includes the terms “Senkachi”, “Tomobiki”, and “Senpu”, and is strongly colored by a syncretism of Shinto and Buddhism. According to research by {{ill|Shigenori Kanda|ja|神田茂|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft}}, the first appearance of the current form of Rokuyō appears to be in the compilation of ''Banreki Ryōmenkan'' (万暦両面鑑) in the fourth year of the {{ill|Enkyō era|ja|延享|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft}} (1747){{Sfn|小池|2021|p=453}}. The assignments for dates in these examples are summarized in the following table: {| class="wikitable" |+ ! rowspan="2" | Lunisolar Calendar Date ! Liu Ren Shikō (time segments) ! Small Liu Ren ! Taian-based Auspicious Day Selection ! Rokuyō |- ! 7th Century ! 1771 ! 1688 ! 1747 |- | January 1 / July 1 | Taian | Small fortune | Taian | Senkachi |- | February 1 / August 1 | Ryūren | Kūbō | Ritsuren | Tomobiki |- | March 1 / September 1 | Sokki | Taian | Zokukichi | Senpu |- | April 1 / October 1 | Shakkō | Ryūren | Shakkō | Butsumetsu |- | May 1 / November 1 | Shōkichi | Sokki | Small fortune | Taian |- | June 1 / December 1 | Kūbō | Shakkō | Kyomō | Shakkō |} == Distribution == Rokuyō follows a repeating cycle in the order “Senkachi → Tomobiki → Senpu → Butsumetsu → Taian → Shakkō.” However, in the lunisolar calendar the Rokuyō for the first day of each month is fixed as follows. In an intercalary month, the assignment remains the same as in the preceding month. {| class="wikitable" |- ! Lunisolar Month ! Rokuyō |- | {{ill|January (Lunisolar)|ja|1月 (旧暦)|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft}} / {{ill|July (Lunisolar)|ja|7月 (旧暦)|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft}} | Senkachi |- | {{ill|February (Lunisolar)|ja|2月 (旧暦)|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft}} / {{ill|August (Lunisolar)|ja|8月 (旧暦)|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft}} | Tomobiki |- | {{ill|March (Lunisolar)|ja|3月 (旧暦)|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft}} / {{ill|September (Lunisolar)|ja|9月 (旧暦)|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft}} | Senpu |- | {{ill|April (Lunisolar)|ja|4月 (旧暦)|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft}} / {{ill|Kannazuki|lt=October (Lunisolar)|ja|10月 (旧暦)|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft}} | Butsumetsu |- | {{ill|May (Lunisolar)|ja|5月 (旧暦)|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft}} / {{ill|November (Lunisolar)|ja|11月 (旧暦)|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft}} | Taian |- | {{ill|June (Lunisolar)|ja|6月 (旧暦)|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft}} / {{ill|December (Lunisolar)|ja|12月 (旧暦)|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft}} | Shakkō |} Thus, in the lunisolar calendar the Rokuyō is determined by the month and day. In essence, if the sum of the lunisolar month number and the day number is a multiple of 6, the day is Taian. However, in solar ({{ill|Solar calendar|ja|新暦|1=New Calendar (Japan)|lt=New Calendar|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft}}) calendars the once-regular cycle may suddenly break, and the Rokuyō for the same day can differ by year or month. This discrepancy between the lunisolar and solar calendars lends an air of mystery to Rokuyō, contributing to its continued use in ceremonial events such as weddings and funerals{{sfn|佐藤|1999|p=226}}. Thus, by applying the modulo operation ({{Math|mod}}) to the sum of the lunisolar month and day numbers, one can easily determine the Rokuyō: {| class="wikitable" style="text-align:center" | colspan="7" | (Month + Day) ÷ 6 = ? … '''Remainder''' |- | '''Remainder''' | '''0'''

1 + 1 = 2, and 2 ÷ 6 leaves a remainder of 2 → Senkachi * Old {{ill|Hina Matsuri|ja|雛祭り|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft}} (March 3 (Lunisolar)): 3 + 3 = 6, and 6 ÷ 6 leaves a remainder of 0 → Taian * Old * Old {{ill|Shichi-Go-San|ja|七五三|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft}} (November 15 (Lunisolar)): 11 + 15 = 26, and 26 ÷ 6 leaves a remainder of 2 → Senkachi === Variation and Arrangement of Rokuyō in Calendars === The way Rokuyō is presented and arranged in calendars reveals the following about the lunisolar calendar: * When one Rokuyō is omitted: ** The day following the omission is usually the first day (the new moon) of a normal (large) month, or it is the first day of an intercalary (small) month if the previous month was small. * When two Rokuyō are omitted: ** The day following the omission is the new moon of a normal month that was a small month. * When Rokuyō continue consecutively for 59 or 60 days: ** The preceding 30 days are from a normal (large) month, and the following 29 or 30 days are from an intercalary month. == Individual Rokuyō == Detailed explanations of each Rokuyō are as follows. The auspicious and inauspicious interpretations currently in use largely derive from the ''Ansei Miscellaneous Wankei Taisei'' (''{{ill|Kojirui-en|ja|古事類苑|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft}}''{{Cite web |title=National Diet Library Digital Collections |url=https://dl.ndl.go.jp/pid/1874246/1/67 |website=dl.ndl.go.jp |access-date=2024-03-31}}). === Senkachi === '''Senkachi''' (先勝 (せんしょう{{sfn|佐藤|1999|p=227}}, sen-kachi{{sfn|佐藤|1999|p=226}})) is considered a day on which it is advantageous to complete tasks early{{sfn|佐藤|1999|p=227}}. Its meaning is “he who acts first wins.” The morning is auspicious, while the afternoon is inauspicious{{sfn|佐藤|1999|p=227}}. It is deemed an auspicious day for handling urgent matters or legal proceedings{{sfn|佐藤|1999|p=227}}. In earlier times it was also written as “Sokki” or “Sokukichi.” === Tomobiki === {{redirect|Tomobiki|Previously, “Tomobiki exclusion” existed in the context of public sports betting (see {{ill|Tickets (Public Sports)|ja|公営競技|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft}}#History).}} '''Tomobiki''' (友引) is regarded as a day on which outcomes—whether favorable or unfavorable—remain undecided{{sfn|佐藤|1999|p=227}}; in some interpretations, the notion of “no win, no loss” or “drawing in friends” renders it auspicious. The term originates from the word “Ryūren” (立連), which originally meant “mutual drawing.” In the context of {{ill|Onmyōdō|ja|陰陽道|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft}}, it referred to days when conducting an activity in a certain direction might bring misfortune upon one’s friends, and this was later conflated with the concept of Tomobiki. The early morning and evening are considered auspicious, while midday is inauspicious{{sfn|佐藤|1999|p=227}}. There is a popular folk belief that funerals should be avoided on Tomobiki days{{sfn|佐藤|1999|p=227}}, as it is thought that holding a funeral on such a day will “draw one’s friends to the underworld” (i.e. lead to death). Consequently, funeral service providers and some crematoria may close on Tomobiki days. However, since Rokuyō is not inherently linked to Buddhism, some Buddhist sects (for example, Jōdo Shinshū) do perform funerals on Tomobiki days. Furthermore, some municipalities have abolished the practice of closing crematoria on Tomobiki days.{{Cite web2 |df=ja |title=Trial of Cremation on Tomobiki Day in Kawasaki City; Responding to an Era of Multiple Deaths |url=https://www.kanaloco.jp/news/government/entry-79466.html |website=神奈川新聞 |date=2016-08-03 |access-date=2024-03-11}}{{Cite web2 |df=ja |title=Deepening Cremation Wait Times in Winter; Chiba City Responds Even on Tomobiki Days |url=https://www3.nhk.or.jp/news/html/20231230/k10014303551000.html |website=NHK News |publisher=NHK |date=2023-12-30 |access-date=2024-03-11}} The superstition to avoid funerals on Tomobiki days is believed to have arisen from a confusion with “Tomobiki” (友曳), which originally referred to a custom of refraining from venturing in the direction indicated by the zodiac sign of that day. Because the sound is the same, the two became conflated. In contexts of celebration, the idea of “no win, no loss” is interpreted as signifying marital harmony; accordingly, some couples schedule their wedding receptions—or send out wedding favors as a “sharing of happiness”—on Tomobiki days. While the reading “Tomobiki” is now standard, its origin lies in the Chinese reading of “留引” as “yūin,” which was then adapted phonetically into Japanese as “Tomobiki,” and is unrelated to the literal meaning “to draw in friends.” The term “留引” originally indicated the persistence or stagnation of an event, suggesting that one should gauge the situation and act accordingly—continuing favorable circumstances or remedying unfavorable ones. === Senpu === {{nihongo|'''Senpu'''|せんぶ{{sfn|佐藤|1999|p=227}}, sen-make{{sfn|佐藤|1999|p=226}}}} is a day on which it is advisable to avoid urgent matters{{sfn|佐藤|1999|p=227}}. It is considered inauspicious for conflicts and official business, and is best suited for maintaining calm in all affairs{{sfn|佐藤|1999|p=227}}. Its meaning, “he who acts first loses,” serves as the counterpart to Senkachi{{sfn|佐藤|1999|p=227}}. The morning is regarded as inauspicious, while the afternoon is considered auspicious{{sfn|佐藤|1999|p=227}}. Originally, it was written as “Small fortune” or “Zhoukichi” and considered an auspicious day, but its present interpretation has prevailed. === Butsumetsu === '''Butsumetsu''' (仏滅) is deemed the most inauspicious day among the Rokuyō. Initially called “Kyobō” (虚亡)—meaning “void” or “no contest,” and also known as “Kūbō” (空亡)—this term later came to be interpreted as signifying the futility of all things, with the character for “Buddha” (仏) being applied to suggest that even the Buddha’s merits are absent{{sfn|佐藤|1999|p=227}}{{Cite Kotobank |word=Butsumetsu |encyclopedia=Heibonsha "Folk Dictionary" |accessdate=2024-03-11}}. However, historical records show that the term “Butsumetsu” first appears in the ''Banreki Ryōmenkan'' compiled in the fourth year of the Enkyō era (1747), while the term “Kyobō” first appears in the ''Ansei Miscellaneous Wankei Taisei'' (1854), prompting some criticism{{Sfn|小池|2021|pp=463-465}}. Butsumetsu is considered inauspicious for all matters{{sfn|佐藤|1999|p=227}}. It is the day on which celebratory events such as weddings are customarily avoided, and as a result some wedding venues offer discounts for ceremonies held on Butsumetsu. While other Rokuyō have multiple readings, Butsumetsu is read only as “butsumetsu.” Because its name includes the character for “Buddha,” it is often mistakenly assumed to represent the day on which the Buddha (Shakyamuni) attained nirvana (i.e. died). In a work from 1819 (''Bunsei Ni-U no Toshi, Nenchū Kiyōkun'uta Zen''), Butsumetsu is already explained as “the day of the Buddha’s death, and therefore unfavorable in every respect”{{sfn|小池|2021|pp=488-490}}. However, Rokuyō is not derived from Buddhism, and the fact that February 15 (lunar calendar)—traditionally regarded as the Buddha’s death anniversary—always falls on Butsumetsu in the lunisolar calendar is merely coincidental. It is also said that this is a day on which one should refrain from all activities, that illnesses tend to worsen, and that Buddhist rites should be avoided. An alternative interpretation under the name “Kyobō” holds that “when things perish and new ones begin, this day is more favorable for starting ventures than Taian.” === Taian === '''Taian''' (大安{{sfn|佐藤|1999|p=226}}) is considered an auspicious day for carrying out any undertaking{{sfn|佐藤|1999|p=227}}. Its name conveys the meaning “great peace and safety.” It is regarded as the most fortunate day among the Rokuyō, ensuring auspiciousness in every endeavor. Derived from the concept of “Tai'an,” many weddings and building ceremonies (such as the {{ill|Jōtōshiki|ja|上棟式|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft}}) are scheduled on Taian days. In addition, some people choose Taian for activities such as car registration, car delivery, construction work on building foundations, or house handovers. === Shakkō === '''Shakkō''' (赤口 (しゃっこう{{sfn|佐藤|1999|p=227}}, shakku{{sfn|佐藤|1999|p=226}})) is considered inauspicious for most of the day except around noon{{sfn|佐藤|1999|p=227}}. Only during the hour of {{ill|Go|ja|午|1=Horse (zodiac)|lt=Horse (午)|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft}} (roughly 11:00 AM to 1:00 PM) is it regarded as auspicious; at all other times, it is deemed inauspicious. It is believed that Shakkō emerged from a conflation of the {{ill|Akashaku-nichi|ja|赤舌日|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft}} of {{ill|Onmyōdō|ja|陰陽道|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft}} and a similar term (sometimes rendered as “Tai-akashaku”), wherein the deity presiding over the western gate of Jupiter (associated with Akashaku-nichi) and the deity presiding over the eastern gate (associated with Shakkō) were both considered inauspicious for legal disputes and contractual agreements{{sfn|佐藤|1999|p=227}}. Because the character for “red” is used in its name, this day is also thought to warn against dangers associated with fire and sharp objects – that is, anything that might symbolically evoke “death.” == Comparison Table of Lunisolar Calendar Dates and Rokuyō == {| class="wikitable" style="float:left;margin:0 1em 1em 0;text-align:right" ! colspan="6" style="background:#ccc" | {{ill|January (Lunisolar)|ja|1月 (旧暦)|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft}} |- ! revision.text:
{{Unreferenced|date=February 2021}} '''Rokuyō''' (六曜) is one of the {{ill|Calendar annotations|ja|暦注|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft}}. It comprises six types of day annotations: '''Senkachi''' (先勝 (せんしょう{{sfn|佐藤|1999|p=227}}, sen-kachi{{sfn|佐藤|1999|p=226}})) – '''Tomobiki''' (友引{{sfn|佐藤|1999|p=226}}) – '''Senpu''' (先負 (せんぷ, せんぶ{{sfn|佐藤|1999|p=227}}, sen-make{{sfn|佐藤|1999|p=226}})) – '''Butsumetsu''' (仏滅{{sfn|佐藤|1999|p=226}}) – '''Taian''' (大安{{sfn|佐藤|1999|p=226}}) – and '''Shakkō''' (赤口 (しゃっこう{{sfn|佐藤|1999|p=227}}, shakku{{sfn|佐藤|1999|p=226}})). == Overview == In {{ill|Japan|ja|日本|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft}}, Rokuyō is one of the most famous {{ill|Calendar|ja|暦|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft}} annotations and is often included in general {{ill|Calendar|ja|カレンダー|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft}} and planner ({{ill|Diary/Planner|ja|手帳|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft}}) publications. It continues to have influence in modern {{ill|Japan|ja|日本|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft}}, where it is linked with ceremonies such as weddings and funerals – for example, it is said that “weddings are best held on {{ill|Taian|ja|大安|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft}}” and “funerals should avoid {{ill|Tomobiki|ja|友引|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft}}.” In calendars based on the seven‐day week, the six annotations are usually printed in full (using two‐character kanji) rather than as abbreviations. However, some calendars highlight only Taian by printing its characters in red or by using a special symbol (such as a circle) to represent it, while omitting the other Rokuyō annotations. It is also known as '''Rokki''' (六輝) or '''Shukuyō''' (宿曜), though these names were coined after the {{ill|Meiji|ja|明治|1=Meiji era|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft}} era to avoid confusion with the seven‐day week system. Although terms such as Butsumetsu and Tomobiki appear to be associated with Buddhist rituals, they are not actually connected to Buddhism. Their seemingly Buddhist character is due to the use of ateji (phonetic substitutions). Since blind reliance on divination may cause one to neglect the essential aspects of a matter – often with adverse consequences – Buddhism rejects such practices. Moreover, in the {{ill|Japanese Buddhism|ja|日本仏教|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft}} of the Jōdo Shinshū sect, Shinran expounded in a {{ill|Wasan|ja|和讃|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft}} that “choosing days based on their auspiciousness or inauspiciousness is not advisable.” Thus, all superstitions and popular beliefs are repudiated, with the understanding that in Buddhism things are determined by causal relationships rather than by Rokuyō. == History == A popular legend claims that Rokuyō originated as the “Kōmei Rokki” conceived by {{ill|Zhuge Liang|ja|諸葛亮|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft}}, though it is doubtful that Rokuyō existed during the {{ill|Three Kingdoms period (China)|ja|三国時代 (中国)|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft}} ({{sfn|佐藤|1999|p=226}}). In general, Rokuyō is believed to have developed as a variation of the Chinese divination system known as {{ill|Liu Ren Divination|ja|六壬神課|lt=Liu Ren Divination|lt_ja=六壬|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft}}.{{Cite web |title=National Diet Library Digital Collections |url=https://dl.ndl.go.jp/pid/1246210/1/124 |website=dl.ndl.go.jp |access-date=2024-03-31}} The “Liu Ren Shikō” (六壬時課) was reportedly devised by {{ill|Li Chunfeng|ja|李淳風|lt=Li Chunfeng|lt_ja=李淳風|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft}} of the {{ill|Tang dynasty|ja|唐|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft}}, and was used to divine the auspiciousness of particular times (i.e. to determine the fortune of a given time period){{Sfn|小池|2021|p=446}}. In Li Chunfeng’s work, ''Rikujin Shōketsu'' (六壬承訣), the days designated include Taian, Ryūren, Sokki, Shakkō, Shōkichi, and Kūbō{{sfn|佐藤|1999|p=226}}. It is thought that Liu Ren Shikō was transmitted to Japan during the {{ill|Muromachi period|ja|室町時代|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft}}, though the details remain uncertain{{Sfn|小池|2021|p=446}}. In China, a day divination method derived from Liu Ren Shikō – known as “Small Liu Ren” (小六壬) – emerged, and was introduced in the {{ill|Qing dynasty|ja|清|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft}} through Chen Zhonghua’s ''Tōdoku Ruijōsho'' (通読類情書) (【1771】){{Sfn|小池|2021|p=457}}. {{ill|Tadao Iijima|ja|飯島忠夫|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft}} considered the Japanese Rokuyō to have evolved from Small Liu Ren. In the fifth year of the {{ill|Jōkyō era|ja|貞享|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft}} (1688), Koizumi Matsutaku (Koizumi Mitsuyasu)’s work 『[https://www.wul.waseda.ac.jp/kotenseki/html/bunko31/bunko31_e1341/index.html Atamae Chōreki]』 featured a diagram for determining auspicious days (“dai an soku kichi jitsu toru no koto”), which assigned Taian (auspicious), Ritsuren (inauspicious), Zokukichi (auspicious), Shakkō (inauspicious), Small fortune (auspicious), and Kyomō (inauspicious){{sfn|佐藤|1999|p=226}}. Although there is a difference between systems that designate auspiciousness for specific times and those that cover whole days, the sequence of annotations is identical to that found in Liu Ren Shikō{{Sfn|小池|2021|pp=447-449}}. The earliest recorded use of the term “Rokuyō” in Japan appears in the ninth year of the {{ill|Genroku period|ja|元禄|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft}} (1696) in a work known as ''Rokuyōshi'' (六曜私) attributed to {{ill|Myōhōin|ja|妙法院|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft}}{{Sfn|小池|2021|p=482}}. Although its relationship to the modern Rokuyō remains unclear, the text includes the terms “Senkachi”, “Tomobiki”, and “Senpu”, and is strongly colored by a syncretism of Shinto and Buddhism. According to research by {{ill|Shigenori Kanda|ja|神田茂|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft}}, the first appearance of the current form of Rokuyō appears to be in the compilation of ''Banreki Ryōmenkan'' (万暦両面鑑) in the fourth year of the {{ill|Enkyō era|ja|延享|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft}} (1747){{Sfn|小池|2021|p=453}}. The assignments for dates in these examples are summarized in the following table: {| class="wikitable" |+ ! rowspan="2" | Lunisolar Calendar Date ! Liu Ren Shikō (time segments) ! Small Liu Ren ! Taian-based Auspicious Day Selection ! Rokuyō |- ! 7th Century ! 1771 ! 1688 ! 1747 |- | January 1 / July 1 | Taian | Small fortune | Taian | Senkachi |- | February 1 / August 1 | Ryūren | Kūbō | Ritsuren | Tomobiki |- | March 1 / September 1 | Sokki | Taian | Zokukichi | Senpu |- | April 1 / October 1 | Shakkō | Ryūren | Shakkō | Butsumetsu |- | May 1 / November 1 | Shōkichi | Sokki | Small fortune | Taian |- | June 1 / December 1 | Kūbō | Shakkō | Kyomō | Shakkō |} == Distribution == Rokuyō follows a repeating cycle in the order “Senkachi → Tomobiki → Senpu → Butsumetsu → Taian → Shakkō.” However, in the lunisolar calendar the Rokuyō for the first day of each month is fixed as follows. In an intercalary month, the assignment remains the same as in the preceding month. {| class="wikitable" |- ! Lunisolar Month ! Rokuyō |- | {{ill|January (Lunisolar)|ja|1月 (旧暦)|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft}} / {{ill|July (Lunisolar)|ja|7月 (旧暦)|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft}} | Senkachi |- | {{ill|February (Lunisolar)|ja|2月 (旧暦)|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft}} / {{ill|August (Lunisolar)|ja|8月 (旧暦)|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft}} | Tomobiki |- | {{ill|March (Lunisolar)|ja|3月 (旧暦)|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft}} / {{ill|September (Lunisolar)|ja|9月 (旧暦)|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft}} | Senpu |- | {{ill|April (Lunisolar)|ja|4月 (旧暦)|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft}} / {{ill|Kannazuki|lt=October (Lunisolar)|ja|10月 (旧暦)|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft}} | Butsumetsu |- | {{ill|May (Lunisolar)|ja|5月 (旧暦)|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft}} / {{ill|November (Lunisolar)|ja|11月 (旧暦)|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft}} | Taian |- | {{ill|June (Lunisolar)|ja|6月 (旧暦)|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft}} / {{ill|December (Lunisolar)|ja|12月 (旧暦)|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft}} | Shakkō |} Thus, in the lunisolar calendar the Rokuyō is determined by the month and day. In essence, if the sum of the lunisolar month number and the day number is a multiple of 6, the day is Taian. However, in solar ({{ill|Solar calendar|ja|新暦|1=New Calendar (Japan)|lt=New Calendar|12=draft|12=draft|12=draft}}) calendars the once-regular cycle may suddenly break, and the Rokuyō for the same day can differ by year or month. This discrepancy between the lunisolar and solar calendars lends an air of mystery to Rokuyō, contributing to its continued use in ceremonial events such as weddings and funerals{{sfn|佐藤|1999|p=226}}.
