Rokuyō | {{color|red|Taian|qq=}} || Shakkō || Senkachi || Tomobiki || Senpu || Butsumetsu || {{color|red|Taian|qq=}} || Shakkō || Senpu || Butsumetsu || {{color|red|Taian|qq=}} || Shakkō || Senkachi || Tomobiki || Senpu |} === Calculating Rokuyō from the Lunisolar Calendar === Unlike the seven‐day week—which requires a complex formula to derive from a Gregorian or Julian date—Rokuyō is uniquely determined by the lunisolar date. Thus, by applying the modulo operation ({{Math|mod|qq=}}) to the sum of the lunisolar month and day numbers, one can easily determine the Rokuyō: {| class="wikitable" style="text-align:center" | colspan="7" | (Month + Day) ÷ 6 = ? … '''Remainder''' |- | '''Remainder''' | '''0'''
Taian | '''1'''
Shakkō | '''2'''
Senkachi | '''3'''
Tomobiki | '''4'''
Senpu | '''5'''
Butsumetsu |} From this, it follows that the following traditional events always occur on the same Rokuyō each year: * {{ill|Lunar New Year|en|Lunar New Year|qid=Q1944136|lt=Lunar New Year}} (January 1 (Lunisolar)): 1 + 1 = 2, and 2 ÷ 6 leaves a remainder of 2 → Senkachi * Old {{ill|Hinamatsuri|en|Hinamatsuri|qid=Q844110|lt=Hina Matsuri}} (March 3 (Lunisolar)): 3 + 3 = 6, and 6 ÷ 6 leaves a remainder of 0 → Taian * Old {{ill|Dragon Boat Festival|en|Dragon Boat Festival|qid=Q1254268|lt=Dragon Boat Festival}} (May 5 (Lunisolar)): 5 + 5 = 10, and 10 ÷ 6 leaves a remainder of 4 → Senpu * Old {{ill|Qixi Festival|en|Qixi Festival|qid=Q13423122|lt=Tanabata}} (July 7 (Lunisolar)): 7 + 7 = 14, and 14 ÷ 6 leaves a remainder of 2 → Senkachi * {{ill|Tsukimi|ja|十五夜|lt=15th Night|lt_ja=月見|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Moon Viewing|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 月見|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q1050292}} (August 15 (Lunisolar)): 8 + 15 = 23, and 23 ÷ 6 leaves a remainder of 5 → Butsumetsu * {{ill|Thirteenth Night|ja|十三夜|lt=13th Night|lt_ja=月見|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Moon Viewing|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q18988720}} (September 13 (Lunisolar)): 9 + 13 = 22, and 22 ÷ 6 leaves a remainder of 4 → Senpu * Old {{ill|Shichi-Go-San|en|Shichi-Go-San|qid=Q1072387|lt=Shichi-Go-San}} (November 15 (Lunisolar)): 11 + 15 = 26, and 26 ÷ 6 leaves a remainder of 2 → Senkachi === Variation and Arrangement of Rokuyō in Calendars === The way Rokuyō is presented and arranged in calendars reveals the following about the lunisolar calendar: * When one Rokuyō is omitted: ** The day following the omission is usually the first day (the new moon) of a normal (large) month, or it is the first day of an intercalary (small) month if the previous month was small. * When two Rokuyō are omitted: ** The day following the omission is the new moon of a normal month that was a small month. * When Rokuyō continue consecutively for 59 or 60 days: ** The preceding 30 days are from a normal (large) month, and the following 29 or 30 days are from an intercalary month. == Individual Rokuyō == Detailed explanations of each Rokuyō are as follows. The auspicious and inauspicious interpretations currently in use largely derive from the ''Ansei Miscellaneous Wankei Taisei'' (''{{ill|Koji Ruien|en|Koji Ruien|qid=Q701081|lt=Kojirui-en}}''{{Cite web |title=National Diet Library Digital Collections |url=https://dl.ndl.go.jp/pid/1874246/1/67 |website=dl.ndl.go.jp |access-date=2024-03-31|qq=}}). === Senkachi === '''Senkachi''' (先勝 (せんしょう{{sfn|佐藤|1999|p=227|qq=}}, sen-kachi{{sfn|佐藤|1999|p=226|qq=}})) is considered a day on which it is advantageous to complete tasks early{{sfn|佐藤|1999|p=227|qq=}}. Its meaning is “he who acts first wins.” The morning is auspicious, while the afternoon is inauspicious{{sfn|佐藤|1999|p=227|qq=}}. It is deemed an auspicious day for handling urgent matters or legal proceedings{{sfn|佐藤|1999|p=227|qq=}}. In earlier times it was also written as “Sokki” or “Sokukichi.” === Tomobiki === {{redirect|Tomobiki|Previously, “Tomobiki exclusion” existed in the context of public sports betting (see {{ill|public gambling|ja|公営競技|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Tickets (Public Sports)|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q11391963}}#History).|qq=}} '''Tomobiki''' (友引) is regarded as a day on which outcomes—whether favorable or unfavorable—remain undecided{{sfn|佐藤|1999|p=227|qq=}}; in some interpretations, the notion of “no win, no loss” or “drawing in friends” renders it auspicious. The term originates from the word “Ryūren” (立連), which originally meant “mutual drawing.” In the context of {{ill|Onmyōdō|en|Onmyōdō|qid=Q1340540|lt=Onmyōdō}}, it referred to days when conducting an activity in a certain direction might bring misfortune upon one’s friends, and this was later conflated with the concept of Tomobiki. The early morning and evening are considered auspicious, while midday is inauspicious{{sfn|佐藤|1999|p=227|qq=}}. There is a popular folk belief that funerals should be avoided on Tomobiki days{{sfn|佐藤|1999|p=227|qq=}}, as it is thought that holding a funeral on such a day will “draw one’s friends to the underworld” (i.e. lead to death). Consequently, funeral service providers and some crematoria may close on Tomobiki days. However, since Rokuyō is not inherently linked to Buddhism, some Buddhist sects (for example, Jōdo Shinshū) do perform funerals on Tomobiki days. Furthermore, some municipalities have abolished the practice of closing crematoria on Tomobiki days.{{Cite web2 |df=ja |title=Trial of Cremation on Tomobiki Day in Kawasaki City; Responding to an Era of Multiple Deaths |url=https://www.kanaloco.jp/news/government/entry-79466.html |website=神奈川新聞 |date=2016-08-03 |access-date=2024-03-11|qq=}}{{Cite web2 |df=ja |title=Deepening Cremation Wait Times in Winter; Chiba City Responds Even on Tomobiki Days |url=https://www3.nhk.or.jp/news/html/20231230/k10014303551000.html |website=NHK News |publisher=NHK |date=2023-12-30 |access-date=2024-03-11|qq=}} The superstition to avoid funerals on Tomobiki days is believed to have arisen from a confusion with “Tomobiki” (友曳), which originally referred to a custom of refraining from venturing in the direction indicated by the zodiac sign of that day. Because the sound is the same, the two became conflated. In contexts of celebration, the idea of “no win, no loss” is interpreted as signifying marital harmony; accordingly, some couples schedule their wedding receptions—or send out wedding favors as a “sharing of happiness”—on Tomobiki days. While the reading “Tomobiki” is now standard, its origin lies in the Chinese reading of “留引” as “yūin,” which was then adapted phonetically into Japanese as “Tomobiki,” and is unrelated to the literal meaning “to draw in friends.” The term “留引” originally indicated the persistence or stagnation of an event, suggesting that one should gauge the situation and act accordingly—continuing favorable circumstances or remedying unfavorable ones. === Senpu === {{nihongo|'''Senpu'''|せんぶ{{sfn|佐藤|1999|p=227|qq=}}, sen-make{{sfn|佐藤|1999|p=226|qq=}}|qq=}} is a day on which it is advisable to avoid urgent matters{{sfn|佐藤|1999|p=227|qq=}}. It is considered inauspicious for conflicts and official business, and is best suited for maintaining calm in all affairs{{sfn|佐藤|1999|p=227|qq=}}. Its meaning, “he who acts first loses,” serves as the counterpart to Senkachi{{sfn|佐藤|1999|p=227|qq=}}. The morning is regarded as inauspicious, while the afternoon is considered auspicious{{sfn|佐藤|1999|p=227|qq=}}. Originally, it was written as “Small fortune” or “Zhoukichi” and considered an auspicious day, but its present interpretation has prevailed. === Butsumetsu === '''Butsumetsu''' (仏滅) is deemed the most inauspicious day among the Rokuyō. Initially called “Kyobō” (虚亡)—meaning “void” or “no contest,” and also known as “Kūbō” (空亡)—this term later came to be interpreted as signifying the futility of all things, with the character for “Buddha” (仏) being applied to suggest that even the Buddha’s merits are absent{{sfn|佐藤|1999|p=227|qq=}}{{Cite Kotobank |word=Butsumetsu |encyclopedia=Heibonsha "Folk Dictionary" |accessdate=2024-03-11|qq=}}. However, historical records show that the term “Butsumetsu” first appears in the ''Banreki Ryōmenkan'' compiled in the fourth year of the Enkyō era (1747), while the term “Kyobō” first appears in the ''Ansei Miscellaneous Wankei Taisei'' (1854), prompting some criticism{{Sfn|小池|2021|pp=463-465|qq=}}. Butsumetsu is considered inauspicious for all matters{{sfn|佐藤|1999|p=227|qq=}}. It is the day on which celebratory events such as weddings are customarily avoided, and as a result some wedding venues offer discounts for ceremonies held on Butsumetsu. While other Rokuyō have multiple readings, Butsumetsu is read only as “butsumetsu.” Because its name includes the character for “Buddha,” it is often mistakenly assumed to represent the day on which the Buddha (Shakyamuni Tathāgata) attained nirvana (i.e. died). In a work from 1819 (''Bunsei Ni-U no Toshi, Nenchū Kiyōkun'uta Zen''), Butsumetsu is already explained as “the day of the Buddha’s death, and therefore unfavorable in every respect”{{sfn|小池|2021|pp=488-490|qq=}}. However, Rokuyō is not derived from Buddhism, and the fact that February 15 (lunar calendar)—traditionally regarded as the Buddha’s death anniversary—always falls on Butsumetsu in the lunisolar calendar is merely coincidental. It is also said that this is a day on which one should refrain from all activities, that illnesses tend to worsen, and that Buddhist rites should be avoided. An alternative interpretation under the name “Kyobō” holds that “when things perish and new ones begin, this day is more favorable for starting ventures than Taian.” === Taian === '''Taian''' (大安{{sfn|佐藤|1999|p=226|qq=}}) is considered an auspicious day for carrying out any undertaking{{sfn|佐藤|1999|p=227|qq=}}. Its name conveys the meaning “great peace and safety.” It is regarded as the most fortunate day among the Rokuyō, ensuring auspiciousness in every endeavor. Derived from the concept of “Tai'an,” many weddings and building ceremonies (such as the {{ill|raising ceremony|ja|上棟式|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Jōtōshiki|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q106351734}}) are scheduled on Taian days. In addition, some people choose Taian for activities such as car registration, car delivery, construction work on building foundations, or house handovers. === Shakkō === '''Shakkō''' (赤口 (しゃっこう{{sfn|佐藤|1999|p=227|qq=}}, shakku{{sfn|佐藤|1999|p=226|qq=}})) is considered inauspicious for most of the day except around noon{{sfn|佐藤|1999|p=227|qq=}}. Only during the hour of {{ill|Horse (zodiac)|ja|午|lt=Horse (午)|2=ja|3=午|lt=Horse (午)|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Go|13=User:Immanuelle/Horse (zodiac)|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q16683439}} (roughly 11:00 AM to 1:00 PM) is it regarded as auspicious; at all other times, it is deemed inauspicious. It is believed that Shakkō emerged from a conflation of the {{ill|Q11635960|ja|赤舌日|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Akashaku-nichi|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q11635960}} of {{ill|Onmyōdō|en|Onmyōdō|qid=Q1340540|lt=Onmyōdō}} and a similar term (sometimes rendered as “Tai-akashaku”), wherein the deity presiding over the western gate of Jupiter (associated with Akashaku-nichi) and the deity presiding over the eastern gate (associated with Shakkō) were both considered inauspicious for legal disputes and contractual agreements{{sfn|佐藤|1999|p=227|qq=}}. Because the character for “red” is used in its name, this day is also thought to warn against dangers associated with fire and sharp objects – that is, anything that might symbolically evoke “death.” == Comparison Table of Lunisolar Calendar Dates and Rokuyō == {| class="wikitable" style="float:left;margin:0 1em 1em 0;text-align:right" ! colspan="6" style="background:#ccc" | {{ill|Zhengyue|en|Zhengyue|qid=Q1072983|lt=January (Lunisolar)}} |- ! Senkachi !! Tomobiki !! Senpu !! Butsumetsu !! Taian !!
